analysis.one_liner: Bans nearly all tobacco advertising, event sponsorship, and branded packaging nationwide.
analysis.headline: The tobacco advertising ban never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee in 1997 with six sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to advertise tobacco products in any form — magazines, billboards, matchbooks, store displays — and illegal for tobacco companies to sponsor sports, music, or entertainment events under their brand names. It would have also required plain packaging: no logos, no pictures, no colors, just black text on a white box. The goal was to cut off the estimated $6 billion a year in tobacco marketing that the bill's findings said draws 3,000 children a day into trying their first cigarette [S3]. The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who are the main targets of tobacco advertising and whose brand preferences are strongly shaped by it; adult smokers trying to quit, who would no longer face constant cigarette marketing; and state and local governments, which the bill expressly allowed to pass their own stricter tobacco rules [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, teens, and smokers trying to quit

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for anyone to advertise tobacco products in newspapers, magazines, billboards, signs, or point-of-purchase displays [S3].
Bars tobacco brands from sponsoring athletic, music, or artistic events, and from putting their brand names on toys, race cars, boats, and sports stadiums [S3].
Requires plain packaging — no brand logos, images, or human figures, with black print on a white background [S3].
Ends free samples, coupons, and other ways to get tobacco products at no or reduced cost [S3].
Explicitly preserves the right of state and local governments to regulate tobacco advertising location and sales, reversing the usual federal preemption that blocks local rules [S3].

Lets federal courts issue injunctions against violators and treats improperly advertised products as misbranded drugs under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, so violations can be stopped quickly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers lose the ability to market at all, ending more than $6 billion a year in promotional spending [S3]. Billboard companies, magazines, and advertising agencies lose tobacco revenue, and sports and entertainment organizations lose sponsorship money. Retailers, especially convenience stores, lose point-of-sale marketing, and newsstands lose a long-standing advertising category.

drawbacks.text: An outright ban on all tobacco advertising goes further than almost any country had done at the time and faced serious First Amendment objections, since commercial speech has some constitutional protection; courts had already struck down some tobacco advertising rules on those grounds.

Magazines, newspapers, billboard companies, and sports organizations would lose substantial advertising and sponsorship income, and some smaller publications dependent on tobacco ads could face real financial pressure.

The bill does nothing about tobacco sales to adults, taxes, or smuggling of unbranded products, so its public health effect depends entirely on whether advertising is the main driver of youth smoking uptake.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is potentially very large: the bill's own findings cite 450,000 deaths and $65 billion in annual costs from smoking, and note that 82 percent of adult smokers started before 18 [S3]. The costs fall on a concentrated set of businesses rather than on consumers directly. The main honest concern is the constitutional one — a total advertising ban may not survive court challenge — but a statute could have been narrowed to survive, and no committee ever took it up to find out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 1997, sent to the Commerce and Judiciary Committees, and referred to the Commerce subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].

narrative.text: Representative James Hansen introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, joined by five cosponsors from both parties [S3][S4].
The Speaker referred it to two committees at once, Commerce and Judiciary, splitting its chances from the start [S5].
On March 7, 1997, the Commerce committee sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, which is the last action recorded for the bill [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers kept the full $6 billion annual marketing machine, and the media, billboard, and sports sponsorship businesses kept tobacco revenue. Teenagers continued to be the target audience for that marketing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and their ad channels

for.name: Rep. James V. Hansen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote findings documenting tobacco's death toll and its $6 billion annual advertising spending [S3].

against.name: House Committee on Commerce leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tobacco advertising
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and sent it to the Health and Environment subcommittee, where it received no hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose advertising the bill would ban
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on the more than $6 billion they spend each year on advertising and promotion; the bill's findings state that 30 years of voluntary agreements with the industry had failed [S3].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican from Utah, with two Republican and three Democratic cosponsors; the bill died quietly in committee without any vote that would have recorded party positions [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would ban all tobacco advertising, promotion, sponsorship, and branded packaging, shutting down the $6 billion annual marketing effort the bill says hooks 3,000 new child smokers a day [S3]. Their product would still be legal, but they could no longer promote it.
Tobacco is a major billboard revenue source; the bill bans tobacco billboards entirely, with two years to comply [S3].
Print tobacco ads would become unlawful, removing significant revenue; the public health rationale puts this media interest against the bill's core purpose.

industries.industry: Sports leagues, race teams, and event promoters
industries.note: Tobacco brand sponsorship of stadiums, race cars, boats, and events would be phased out as existing contracts end, costing these organizations a funding stream while removing tobacco branding from venues children attend [S3].
